en: Sutta Nipāta 4.12 Cūḷabyūhasutta “Clinging each to his own respective view, they do not understand.”
Engaging in dispute, those skilled in various doctrines speak;
he who knows thus has understood the Dhamma,
while he who rejects this is incomplete.
Thus they quarrel and dispute, saying,
"The other is a fool, he is unskilled.
Of these, which statement is the true one?
"For all these are indeed proponents of the wholesome.
"But the fool who does not approve of the Dhamma of another is base and of inferior wisdom."
All these fools are of utterly inferior wisdom;
all of them are thoroughly ensnared by views.
They are not purified even regarding what is directly visible.
Those of purified wisdom, skillful and possessed of insight—
none among them have lost their wisdom,
for their views are likewise fully perfected.
I do not say that what fools call "truth" to one another is true;
each has made their own respective view the truth.
"Therefore, they burn others,
saying, 'This one is a fool. "What some call truth and reality,
others call empty and false."
"Even so, having delved into the matter, they dispute:
'Why do the recluses not speak with one voice?
For there is but one truth, and no second."
In that which people who understand do not dispute,
yet they themselves proclaim various truths;
therefore, the ascetics do not speak with one voice.
“Why indeed do they speak of truths diversely?
You who profess yourselves skilled in speech,
why do you proclaim so many diverse truths that have been heard?”
"Or do they merely recollect their own reasoning?
"No, for there are not many diverse truths in the world,
other than that [the world] perceives things as permanent."
Having formed a conceptualization regarding views, they speak of two things: truth and falsehood.
Whether in what is seen, heard, in moral conduct and vows, or in what is sensed;
Relying on these, he dwells in his celestial mansion;
standing in judgment, he laughs and says,
"The other is a fool, unskilled."
By the very fact that he despises another as a fool,
he says of himself, "I am skilled";
thus, by his own account, he proclaims himself to be one who is skilled.
He despises another, yet he himself is just like that.
Perfected by the view of extreme asceticism,
intoxicated by conceit, he is full of pride.
One who has been consecrated by one's own mind alone—
that is indeed his view, being thus fully perfected.
But if one is inferior due to the word of another, [that view is not truly his].
One who is dull-witted is dull-witted even when accompanied by others;
but if one is oneself a wise sage,
there is no fool among the recluses.
Those who profess a doctrine other than this have missed purity, for they are not complete;
even so do the various sectarians speak.
For they are stained by attachment to what is visible here and now;
they proclaim purity in this very world,
and do not speak of purification through other teachings.
Thus do the various sectarians remain settled in their own doctrines,
asserting them there with firm conviction;
and even one who asserts his own doctrine with firm conviction—
Why then should a fool burn another?
He brings that very destruction upon himself by speaking of another as a fool whose nature is impure.
Standing in judgment and being himself negligent,
he incurs disputes in this world and the next;
having abandoned all forms of judgment, [he is free from strife].
A person does not create a fever in the world.
Thus ends the twelfth sutta, the Cūḷabyūhasutta.
